Farid al-Din Attar speaks of the Simurgh in these lines, here given in their sense:

At the beginning, the Simurgh showed a wondrous glimpse of itself, Passing over China in the middle of the night. One feather fell there, and the whole world was stirred. Each person took an image from that feather; Whoever saw the image was filled with longing. All the works of creation shine by its splendour; Every image is an image from its feather. If the feather's image had not appeared, All this commotion would never have arisen. That feather is now in the picture-house of China: This is the meaning of “Seek knowledge, even in China.”

The bird appearing in China stands for the universal intellect. China stands for the universal heavenly soul, at the farthest eastern reach of the spiritual world. Night is the descending order of existence, the reality expressed by the Night of Power. The fallen feather is a reflection or shadow of the intellect; the kingdoms are the turning heavens; and the image each person receives is the particular intellect.

Attar also says that we have a king beyond Mount Qaf, named the Simurgh, king of birds: “He is close to us, and we are far from him.” Those lines point more clearly to existence flowing through all things.
Here, “what is present to the soul” means its good or bad traits and habits.
One version of the text reads “clustered fruit” here.
Avicenna compares the soul's connection to this body to a mirror's connection to images: the body lets familiar images appear to the soul.
Avicenna holds that matter and form always go together. He does not accept forms that exist independently of matter.

The note describes the old medical view that the soul is connected to the body through subtle vapors and the body's vital spirit, which flows through the arteries, nerves, and veins, especially in the heart, brain, and liver.

Seeing happens when an image appears in the inner sense called the phantasia, which works like a two-sided mirror. An image may come from the outer senses or arise within. The inner sense receives it, and imagination keeps it. The images coming from within may be reflections of spiritual realities or forms assembled by imagination from what it has stored.

The note argues that an image gives pleasure because it appears to the soul, not because it exists in matter outside us. A beautiful image in matter exists for that matter, not for us. If a child dies or leaves, the outside event does not by itself cause our pain; the image we form of it does. The note alludes to the story of Khidr and Moses.
The “market” is the good habits formed by repeating good actions. Each habit is a real counterpart to a particular subtle form.
The next life's images come into being through direct creation, while things here are formed from matter.
The note refers to the creation of likenesses and forms in the next life, and to Qur'anic statements about things we do not know. These, the author argues, point beyond the materialist account.
The peaceful soul returns to God; other souls draw near to Him. For those who are far from Him, nearness reveals His power and majesty.

The author repeats an old medical account in which semen forms from vapors rising through the body and gathering at its extremities. The note says this account was used to explain why cutting veins behind the ears was thought to affect fertility.
These are rhetorical arguments about God's power, not strict demonstrations.

The question of how parts join or separate is obvious and needs no proof. Materialists ascribe it to natural powers, while Ash'arite theologians ascribe it to God alone. The author argues that natural powers are themselves fields of divine action; the real issue is the goal toward which beings move and the realm to which they return.

The next realm is not beside this world; it stands above it in the order of existence. Until we leave the veils of the natural body, we are not yet in the afterlife. The note compares this transition to a chick emerging from its egg.

If nothing continually sustained composite things, their parts would separate as the elements moved toward their natural places. Earlier, the author argued that God must hold them together against those tendencies.

“Bodies” here includes both natural bodies and the imaginal bodies of the afterlife. Natural bodies are like graves or coverings for imaginal forms and souls. A Persian couplet says that when Israfil blows his trumpet, the dead souls rise.

Animals can be raised by following human beings in two ways: all the things attached to a person may follow them, or perfected animal forms may return to the imaginal realm while the soul returns to a luminous, intellectual form. In either case, they return to God in their own way.
This means that they follow the human journey in its vertical order of stages.

The verses include those in The Event, “Is the One who created the heavens and earth not able to create others like them?”, and “Who will give life to these bones when they have decayed? Say: The One who brought them into being the first time.” The note says the first creation came directly from the active cause, without pre-existing matter, and so can resurrection.
The author will take up these objections one at a time and answer them later.
That is, more fitting to God's own nature.
The whole natural world is created. Matter, time, and space do not themselves depend on earlier matter, time, or space; every kind of thing born within the world is created.
The imaginal realm is timelessly prior to the material world; the intellectual realm is prior in its own order and in timeless rank. For those nearest to God, it is the highest goal.
The imaginal realm comes later only in relation to our own existence.
This differs from the view of some religious scholars, who say that paradise and hell will not be created until the final resurrection.

There are two blasts: one puts out a fire and the other lights one. Our natural bodies are like pieces of wood burning with a fire that is God's light. At the great resurrection this fire is extinguished all at once, while other pieces of wood—pure forms belonging to the next life—are lit by the souls to which they belong. Those forms become the bodies of that life.

Look at the order of things from beginning to end. At one time the lights that govern souls are joined to material bodies; at another they are joined to the pure forms of the next life. In a limited way, this resembles our present experience: while awake, our souls are attached to natural bodies, but in sleep they appear through bodies of images. Scripture says that God takes souls at death, and also those that have not died during their sleep; He keeps those for whom death is decreed and sends the others back.

To understand the point, consider where human beings—and indeed all animals—come from. Their bodily material goes back to the elements. Those elements have no life, knowledge, power, or other perfection of their own. Such qualities arrive in them as gifts held for a time, and one day those gifts must be returned. While looking at a living body in all its splendour, remember the same materials when they are lifeless and disfigured. That contrast shows where its passing bodily life begins.

Naturalists recognize passive and natural powers but miss the active causes that act through them. They also fail to recognize imaginal souls and separate intellects. Materialists who appeal to time as the cause of life, death, union, and separation likewise fail to recognize the immaterial self within them or God beyond them.

The author calls the view that affirms both kinds of resurrection the soundest. A human being is body and soul, and each has its fitting completion and reward. A purely spiritual afterlife would leave most people without a suitable goal; a purely bodily afterlife would fail to account for the highest souls.

“This body” means the imaginal body of the next life. The same person persists through the form, not through the same matter. The soul gives the body its individuality, and its own individuality is grounded in its real existence and unity.

This objection assumes that a person is identified by the body's matter and is restored by gathering the same material pieces. If identity belongs to the body's form, material from one body can become part of another body without the person's form transferring. Food becomes part of the eater's body, but the food's form does not. Every form remains itself for its own time; it does not turn into another form. A body, as a body, does not become food for something else. Matter is called the matter of a body only because it is joined to that body's form.

The note rejects the idea that a person's identity lies in their matter. It belongs to their form. A person has an inner form—the soul—and an outer bodily form. Both remain in the next life, so the person's identity is preserved.

The point is whether the human being survives, not whether an abstract idea of “body” survives. A body as a general kind exists only through real, particular bodies. The note discusses the claim that a body's continuity may remain the same even as it is divided, but rejects this as incomplete: the body's basic form and connection come before its other kinds of continuity.

This objection applies even if there are souls besides the one that belonged to the body. If an infinite number of souls existed, they would crowd and block one another, since a limited world cannot hold an unlimited number. Theologians who say that souls are finite do not face this particular problem.
A proverb says: “Look to the goals; leave the beginnings.”

According to Plato's followers, every kind of thing, even water, earth, air, fire, gold, silver, and other minerals, has an intellectual form. This makes all beings copies of those forms. The note says it is a serious weakness that they do not allow for a closer, subtle version of these forms in the world between matter and intellect.

The difference between the two interpretations is clear. In the first, the intellectual realities are the same kind of thing as their subtle counterparts, differing only in how broad or limited they are. In the second, they are inner states and qualities of the soul, different in meaning from outside things, like the difference between greenness and flowing water. The first view treats them as real forms; the second treats them as results or meanings that these forms bring about.

The note says this argument completes the account of pleasure, not pain. An effect like poison may become a noble, bright intellectual experience when it is understood. The intellectual world is a world of beauty, truth, and clarity; this reading returns to the first interpretation, though the commentator notes that it has problems.

The commentator asks how a bodily effect, such as touch, could become an intellectual experience while remaining a touch. This could make sense only if “touch” means intellectual awareness, and the intellectual form is like the bodily form of touch.
The note says the lover had many beloved things: women, children, gold, silver, fine horses, and other worldly goods.

“Imaginal” here does not mean a weak picture that has no reality. The author is careful to say that the afterlife forms are not merely in human imagination. They have real existence in the imaginal world.

This is especially clear in the view that mirror images belong to the imaginal world. An afterlife image is like a mirror image, but it exists on its own, without a mirror, and is alive through its connection to the soul.

In sleep and similar states, the soul's power to perceive is also its power to create. The sky, ground, people, and other things seen in a dream are made by the soul without matter and are directly present to it.
The word here is a broken plural. The note says the soul's world can include many levels: the two worlds, their joined whole, and a still wider realm beyond them.
In The Healing, Avicenna says that the true religious law has already explained bodily resurrection, while he will explain spiritual resurrection himself.

This view is better because it does not reduce a human being to bones, muscles, veins, and flesh. It allows for an immaterial spirit as well. But its supporters have not fully explained what the returning bodies are, what they are like, or where they exist, and they have not explained the final state of the higher souls.

The Torah mostly contains laws and teachings about conduct, with little about God's oneness, names, qualities, or the afterlife. The Qur'an treats these subjects in much greater detail. The note suggests that the Torah's time in paradise may refer to the period when believers enjoy bodily pleasures before moving into a spiritual life. The Gospel's account may describe the spiritual afterlife of the righteous and those close to God.

Each person returns alone, as an individual apart from matter and its attachments. For some, this means being alone apart from their nature and its qualities as well. A Persian verse says: “Yesterday, the day before, and today—all four become one when you become one.”

This refers to souls who have completed their practical development but not their intellectual development. They reach an intermediate world, unlike those who have completed both forms of growth and hold the highest rank.
Trees, rivers, rooms, the sky, the earth, the speaker, and the listener seen in dreams or sudden visions are all forms of awareness, strong or weak.

The first two principles show that what returns after death is the individual's own particular existence. Since existence is what makes a person this person, identity remains even when many features and forms change. Distinguishing features may change as different expressions of one continuing individual.

The third principle works together with the fourth. Strength and weakness, and the gradual movement from one to the other, are not separate kinds of existence. The same existence can grow from something hardly noticeable into a simple intellect and an active intellect. The more complete stage remains the very existence that was less complete, just as the dust can become, by stages, the Lord of all worlds.
Saying that a lower level of existence is “base” does not mean existence is evil. Existence is good and noble. Here, “base” means a lower and less complete level, not the absence of existence.

The unity of one continuous motion is its personal unity. It is one as a whole, although it has points and stages along the distance it covers. Its continuity is simple; change and multiplicity come from its relation to these points and stages.

Some of these principles are necessary for the argument, while others help establish it. This one is especially important. “Form” here includes a thing's kind, bodily form, arrangement, or whatever makes it actual, such as the soul that makes an animal an animal.

If the composite is what it is through its form and final difference, one might wonder why definitions of composites list many broader kinds and differences. The author distinguishes two tasks: showing how one thing contains many parts, and showing how many parts form one thing. Detailed definitions serve the first task. His account serves the second: once a thing is complete, the features named in its definition follow from its form rather than existing separately from it.
This returns to the earlier claim that a defining feature is a way of existing. It also refers to the author's choice among four accounts of how a thing's inner conceptual parts are combined.

“This” refers to the meaning of Avicenna's claim. The note asks how defining something by features that follow from it can compare with defining it by the parts and causes that make it what it is. The reply is that features that do not come later than the thing in existence disclose its inner reality. On the view that existence is primary, all essences are drawn from existence itself; essence and existence are united rather than joined as separate parts.

This, too, is a necessary principle. The soul is one, yet it contains many powers and has a kind of unity through them, just as it has multiplicity within its unity. It is a wonder among beings, and its unity a wonder among kinds of unity: it is one while containing all multiplicities and worlds. “The greater world is folded within you.” Everything sensed, imagined, supposed, or understood—including pleasures and pains, actions and traits, and particular and general meanings—is a state or aspect of the soul. The many things are really concepts drawn from the levels of its existence. The soul has a reflected, dependent unity; God's unity is real and not numerical. The note ends with a Persian verse: “How did the shadow stretch? It is the pattern of the saints, showing the light of God's sun.”

The soul's rising and descending through these levels does not mean it moves from one physical place to another. In its simple intellective reality it is in the world beyond nature and in timeless duration; in its natural body it is in the material world and in time.
The soul and intellect are therefore distinct kinds of substance within the five traditional categories of substance.

Saying that individuation comes from existence does not by itself explain the body. The body is individuated through the soul, while the soul is individuated through its existence. Not all philosophers held that individuation comes from existence, but many accepted that the body is individuated through the soul; this helps explain how the resurrected body and the body in this life can retain one identity.
The answer also relies on the claim that the soul preserves the body's identity.
The imaginative power works together with the common sense, which perceives. Imagination stores and preserves the forms it perceives.

The point is that different forms can arise from the active cause rather than from differences in the matter receiving them. For example, images of a person, horse, or tree reflected in water differ because of the reflecting causes, even though the water is one kind of matter. Likewise, kinds of things can arise from different aspects of their active causes. In some philosophical accounts, intellectual beings are the active causes of natural kinds; in others, those kinds arise from divine ideas. Each form is a creative divine word: “Be!” The things corresponding to those forms exist through God's necessary existence, while created forms exist through possible existence.

“The power that forms images” means the common sense considered from its inward side. As explained earlier, it is like a mirror with two faces: it perceives forms from imagination and forms assembled by the image-making power, while imagination preserves them. “Image-making power” can also mean imagination or, more commonly, one of the four principal plant powers.

Imagined forms can serve as mirrors through which we look at something else. When the mind attends to the sun outside us—its brightness, eclipse, or other features—the imagined image is only a reflected appearance of that physical sun. When the image itself becomes the object of awareness, however, it is a real being in its own right, more complete because it is free of matter. It is like an immaterial sun: a universal intellectual reality that contains all its limited, passing instances. The universal concept of the sun is a light that lets the intellect know all the individual suns. While the soul is busy with individual things and its body and powers draw its attention to desirable objects, the universal concept may seem weak. But its weakness is not part of its own nature. The same is true of an imaginal form.
Unlike the intellectual mode, which is universal and free of matter, the individual mode consists of measured imaginal forms. In the primordial world, these are the forms of the covenant.

“Clay” can mean a thing's essence, the settled qualities that shape the rational soul, or the matter of the body. For the prophets, the virtuous and their followers, these meanings refer to their complete human nature, their good qualities and habits, and the balanced bodily mixture formed in pure lineages and wombs. For hypocrites and their followers, the contrasts are a merely potential humanity, blameworthy qualities and habits, and an unbalanced bodily mixture.
This means whether their bodies are imaginal or physical.
That is, when the person's substantial development, together with the changing qualities that follow it, reaches its full course during worldly life.

The word for “nurse” is Persian. The commentator explains the image: nature is the mother; plant and animal life are its two breasts. Because the human body is delicate, the elements cannot nourish it without being changed by nature and, at times, by human craft. Just as a baby needs its mother's milk rather than adult food, the bodily human being receives nourishment through plant and animal life. The spiritual human being also needs knowledge from two sources—the theoretical and practical intellect—as nourishment for growth and completion.
The commentator suggests that the text may have read, “You already know…” without labeling the passage “the eleventh principle.”

“Imaginal” here means a real, distinct form in the world of images, not merely a separate body made of different matter. The author says that existence, individuality, soul, and form are truly what they are, even as they become stronger and more complete. A stronger stage is the same individual as the weaker stage; it does not become a second individual or kind. In the next life, only limitations and defects are removed. Pure capacity, which is not yet an actual feature of a person, falls away. Otherwise, the form would remain worldly rather than becoming an afterlife form.

In the language of revelation, resurrection means arrival at one's final ends; in the language of philosophy, it means reaching those ends. “Resurrection” is used in scripture for arrival at ends beyond what the senses can perceive. The soul's imaginal form and change of meaning are part of this movement.

The final end gathers together the ends of all things. God has beautiful names that guide each kind and its proper end; all the levels of the worlds express His power and knowledge. The ends of people devoted to inner meaning and of people devoted to outward form are both with Him: He has a place of welcome for some and a place of punishment for others.

The spiritually advanced have already reached their end through the strength of their awareness of God. Their simple intellect and universal divine soul belong to the world beyond nature even while their bodies remain in the material world. Their true time is timeless duration, and what is fixed in relation to what is fixed belongs to eternity. When the body's covering is removed, this state appears fully. This is like the report that Ali said, “By the Lord of the Kaaba, I have won,” and also said, “If the veil were lifted, my certainty would not increase.” The same applies to the passage about driving the guilty onward.

If “animals” means nonhuman animals, their resurrection is dependent on the human one; paradise contains birds and other creatures that souls desire. If it means people who are like sheep and gazelles in their ignorance, then their gathering is direct. Likewise, “stars” may mean low-growing plants, and “trees” plants with trunks; or both may refer to people whose life has remained at the level of plant life, occupied only with taking in and expelling, and deeply attached to plants.

The shape of food does not matter to nourishment. Bread becomes part of the person who eats it, but it first changes through several stages into pure blood. Its roundness, length, or other shape does not become part of the eater. If a form itself became food, it would no longer be that form while serving as food.
The increase in size comes through expansion: the amount grows without adding more basic material parts. This is what the commentator calls true expansion.

The first answer is based on proof. The second is only a debate within the assumption that the resurrected body must be a natural body of finite size. Even if the spiritually advanced are no longer connected to bodies, the number of other souls is still unlimited. God's giving is without end, whether for those brought near, those on the right, those on the left, or those between them. The infinite cannot be measured by the finite.

A complete world contains everything necessary to its existence and its consequences. If it were made from the matter of this natural world, it would compete with other forms for that matter and depend on them, so it would not be complete. If it occupied a place and position here, it would be surrounded by the world's places and directions, and depend on them. It would not be self-sufficient. The next life is not alongside this world in the same time sequence; its mode is timeless. Those who ask when the Hour will come do not understand the answer “Its knowledge is with my Lord,” because they have not entered the divine presence. The final ends of the worlds are within this world in depth, as stations of truth before the Sovereign, especially in the presence of God and the realm of His names and attributes. The next world contains forms of everything, including places, times, positions, and directions, but they belong to its own mode of existence.

This is like the verse, “My Lord, send me back, so that I may do good.” Another way a person can speak with God is by becoming a stronger expression of His qualities and receiving His creative words more fully.

The motion and change that produce the soul are those in which each later stage gathers the perfections of the earlier one and adds something more. It is not the mere exchange of one bodily garment for another, nor a downward movement of matter. Matter has descended to its lowest form; how could the rational soul remain naturally connected to it so that it prevented a new soul from arising, as the argument claims?

“Like a heavenly body” refers to its delicacy, clarity, luminosity, and balanced mixture. When opposites are balanced, each is present in a way that resembles its absence. Because of these similarities, one term can stand for the other: the life-giving spirit may be called a heaven, and the heavens may be called vapor or smoke, as in the verse: “Then He turned toward the heaven while it was smoke.”

The soul is what makes a person an individual. If old Zayd is the same as young Zayd because the soul preserves their identity, he is also the same person as the fetus. The resurrected person is therefore the very one who obeyed or disobeyed.
The commentator says that resurrection restores the human form a person had in the first life, whereas transmigration would give the soul an animal form.

If the soul alone individuates a person, as that account says, but resurrection restores the first individual while transmigration makes another, the account seems to require an additional feature—such as the new and old forms matching—to explain identity.
The same soul also remains through transmigration, so on this account it would preserve individuality there as well.

The commentator says this is especially strange for two reasons: Ghazali says the returning body shares no parts with the first body, even though he distinguishes resurrection as the return of the first person; and he allows a kind of transmigration while strongly condemning it elsewhere.
This is the view of those who believe in transmigration: after a soul leaves its body, it enters, for example, an embryo in an animal's womb.
Here, “this” refers to the alleged impossibility of transmigration.

The idea that a heavenly body becomes the setting for a soul's imagination does not mean the soul becomes its soul. The commentator says that Ghazali's reading of Avicenna suggests uncertainty about transmigration because he thinks the heavenly body becomes the soul's own body.

If a soul were inside the body as an accident is inside its subject, it would not be independent enough to have a relation to two possible bodies. A soul free of matter can have such relations without being contained in either body.
